orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the October 7, 2016 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on water on a stairway in defendants’ owned building. The source and duration of the water are unstated.

legal_issues.finding: General cleaning/inspection practices did not establish specific inspection, cleaning or duration. A minutes-or-seconds deposition theory was speculative, and gaps in plaintiff’s proof could not satisfy defendants’ burden.

quality.notes: Explicit ownership supports private premises; building use, role/date and evidence format unknown. Water-deposition theory concerns when water appeared, not testimony. General notice language is resolved through constructive notice, not a separate actual-notice ruling.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell on water on a stairway in a building owned by the defendants.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Wade, J.), dated October 7, 2016, which denied their motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, the defendants did not submit any evidence regarding specific cleaning or inspection of the area in question, or any other affirmative proof to demonstrate how long the condition had existed. Rather, they merely provided evidence regarding the general cleaning practices and inspection procedures employed by the building superintendent, which is insufficient to establish a lack of constructive notice

Further, the defendants' contention that the "water could have been deposited there only minutes or seconds before the alleged fall" is pure speculation, and the defendants cannot satisfy their initial burden on summary judgment merely by pointing to gaps in the plaintiff's case

Since the defendants failed to demonstrate their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, the Supreme Court properly denied their motion without regard to the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition papers

orders.description: Plaintiff’s limited appeal from the August 18, 2020 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted CPLR 3211 dismissal of the amended complaint against Panini based on release.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell while working at Panini’s restaurant in August 2018. He later signed an employment separation agreement and general release in April 2019; the fall location within the restaurant and hazard are unstated.

legal_issues.finding: The general release unambiguously covered this personal-injury claim arising from plaintiff’s employment and barred it against Panini. Remaining plaintiff contentions were rejected without detail.

evidence_discussed.description: Executed separation agreement/general release discharged employment-related claims including tort claims; construed to cover this action.

quality.notes: Include substantive release defense disposing of the direct premises-injury claim; CPLR 3211 vehicle alone is not procedural-only. No negligence finding, workers’ compensation defense, fraud/duress fact or accident day inferred. August 2018 is partial date. Unchanged rules for 2024 opinion; human review should check release-based scope.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

The plaintiff commenced this action against, among others, the defendant Panini La Cafe, Inc., a restaurant in Brooklyn (hereinafter Panini), to recover damages for personal injuries he alleged he sustained in August 2018, when he slipped and fell while working at Panini.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Kathy J. King, J.), dated August 18, 2020. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted that branch of the motion of the defendant Panini La Cafe, Inc., which was pursuant to CPLR 3211 (a) to dismiss the amended complaint insofar as asserted against it.

In April 2019, the plaintiff's employment with Panini was terminated and, in connection therewith, he executed a confidential separation agreement and general release (hereinafter the release). According to the release, the plaintiff discharged Panini, inter alia, from "any and all . . . causes of action of any kind whatsoever in tort, contract, by statute, or any other basis," which the plaintiff "ever had, now has or may have" against Panini "arising out of [the plaintiff's] employment relationship with" Panini.

Here, the release covered any and all claims, including the cause of action set forth in this personal injury action. The plaintiff's remaining contentions are without merit. Accordingly, the release bars the action insofar as asserted against Panini

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the January 5, 2015 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s summary-judgment motion and dismissed the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on snow or ice in defendant’s parking lot. She argued snowfall was light and presented a property-management expert criticizing snow/ice removal practices.

legal_issues.finding: Snow/ice remediation duty was suspended until a reasonable period after the storm ended.
Plaintiff failed to raise an issue that the fall involved a preexisting condition with actual or constructive notice; neither category was independently conclusively found.
Plaintiff failed to raise an issue that the fall involved a preexisting condition with actual or constructive notice; neither category was independently conclusively found.
Defendant established an ongoing storm; light snowfall did not defeat the rule, and plaintiff failed to raise a preexisting-condition-with-notice issue.
Property-management expert’s customary-practices criticism did not raise an issue because storm conditions suspended the removal duty.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s property-management expert criticized removal practices; submission format unspecified.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ORDERED that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.
Plaintiff commenced this action seeking damages for injuries she sustained when she slipped and fell on snow or ice in defendant’s parking lot.
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Monroe County (Thomas A. Stander, J.), entered January 5, 2015. The order granted the motion of defendant for summary judgment and dismissed the complaint.

“Defendant met its initial burden by establishing that a storm was in progress at the time of the accident and, thus, that it ‘had no duty to remove the snow [or] ice until a reasonable time ha[d] elapsed after cessation of the storm’ ” (Witherspoon v Tops Mkts., LLC, 128 AD3d 1541, 1541).

In opposition to the motion, plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact “whether the accident was caused by a slippery condition at the location where the plaintiff fell that existed prior to the storm, as opposed to precipitation from the storm in progress, and that the defendant had actual or constructive notice of the preexisting condition” (Meyers v Big Six Towers, Inc., 85 AD3d 877, 878).
Contrary to plaintiff’s contention, evidence that it was only snowing lightly at the time of the accident does not render the storm in progress doctrine inapplicable.

The assertions of plaintiff’s property management expert that defendant’s snow and ice removal practices deviated from accepted and customary practices of property management also failed to raise an issue of fact, inasmuch as “defendant’s duty in this regard was suspended until a reasonable period of time after the storm ended” -2- 1339 CA 15-00518 (Wood v Converse, 263 AD2d 860, 861).

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the February 5, 2013 order.

facts.factual_summary: While visiting defendant’s home on August 8, 2010, plaintiff allegedly caught her toe on the elevated side of a door saddle between dining room and hallway. Photographs she authenticated showed elevation of less than half an inch.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant established triviality without trap/nuisance characteristics using the circumstances, testimony and photographs; plaintiff raised no factual issue.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition authenticated photographs as depicting the accident-time saddle condition.
Authenticated photographs showed less than half-inch elevation and supported triviality.

quality.notes: Defendant’s private home supports control without expressly assigning title. Interior doorway is indoor_floor, not external entrance. No code, notice or open-and-obvious finding; the opinion does not set a universal half-inch rule.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

On August 8, 2010, the plaintiff, while visiting the defendant’s home, allegedly was injured when she tripped and fell over a door saddle situated in a doorway between the dining room and the first floor hallway. According to the plaintiff, the accident occurred as she was walking from the dining room toward the hallway when the big toe of her left foot became caught on the left side of the door saddle, which was elevated, causing her to lose her balance and fall.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Bruno, J.), dated February 5, 2013, which granted the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

In support of his motion, he relied upon, among other things, the plaintiffs deposition testimony and photographs, which the plaintiff testified accurately depicted the condition of the saddle at the time of the accident. Those photographs showed that the elevation of the left side of the saddle was less than one half of one inch.

Here, the defendant established, prima facie, his entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that the alleged defect, which did not have any characteristics of a trap or nuisance, was trivial and, therefore, not actionable
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Perez’s limited appeal from the September 28, 2020 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied dismissal of the complaint against Perez.

facts.factual_summary: Decedent allegedly slipped on a wet metal step while entering the tenant’s liquor store on July 14, 2016. Perez owned the building; the source of the wetness and decedent’s role are unstated.

legal_issues.finding: Perez failed to negate contractual responsibility for premises including the metal step; this does not conclusively establish a duty or breach.
Perez failed to establish out-of-possession status with no contractual maintenance duty because he omitted the lease from initial submissions; submitting it in reply did not cure the failure.
Lease first submitted in reply could not satisfy the initial summary-judgment burden.

evidence_discussed.description: Lease omitted from moving papers, then provided in reply too late to establish initial entitlement; terms not adopted as facts.

quality.notes: Express owned building and leased store entry support private premises. Wet-step hazard is coded water without inferring a source, weather or structural defect. No customer role inferred. Ancillary reply-paper rule accompanies substantive landlord-duty defense. Unchanged rules for 2022 opinion.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

On July 14, 2016, the plaintiff's decedent allegedly sustained personal injuries when he slipped and fell on a wet metal step as he entered a liquor store operated by the defendant Los Compadres Liquors and Wines (hereinafter the tenant). The liquor store was located in a building owned by the defendant Isidro Perez.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant Isidro Perez appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Jerome C. Murphy, J.), entered September 28, 2020. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied that branch of that defendant's motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him.

Here, in support of his motion, Perez failed to provide a copy of the lease agreement between himself and the tenant. Consequently, Perez failed to establish, prima facie, that he was an out-of-possession landlord who lacked any contractual obligation to maintain the premises, including [*2] the metal step at issue
Furthermore, contrary to Perez's contention, he could not sustain his prima facie burden by relying on the copy of the lease agreement that he submitted for the first time with his reply papers

Accordingly, since Perez failed to establish his prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, the Supreme Court properly denied that branch of his motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him, regardless of the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition papers
